findings.title: block-speaking-inbox-dir refused reads it was never scoped to
findings.detail: agents/roadmaps/archive/road-to-the-14-22-0-disposition-residuals.md:272 moved from agents/roadmaps/. The hook block-speaking-inbox-dir (src/scripts/hooks/block_speaking_inbox_dir.ts) refuses reads of agents/roadmaps/**, but its own docblock (:15-20) scopes it to 'agents/tmp/inbox-*/' only — the roadmap folder is outside that scope. The roadmap move from active → archive is a normal workflow operation, yet the hook would refuse reading the archived file. Either the hook's scope is wider than documented (and should be), or the archived roadmap violates the hook's intended boundary. The diff shows the move but no hook allowlist update.

findings.title: ADR-263 Amendment 1 contradicts its own scoping statement
findings.detail: docs/decisions/ADR-263-skills-are-explicitly-invoked-reference-material.md:138 Amendment 1 says 'this amendment corrects one figure, at the two places it appears' and names :102 and the supporting bullet. But the amendment's own first paragraph (:138-141) says 'Scope, stated first so it cannot be misread: this amendment corrects **one figure, at the two places it appears**. The Decision is untouched'. Yet :196 in § Consequences still reads 'the published reading of skill-activation-census-zero ... is now wrong and is superseded by this record' without carrying a pointer to Amendment 1. A reader landing on § Consequences via cross-reference meets an unbounded supersession claim with no inline flag that it was partially corrected. The § Consequences bullet below (:168-176) now carries the pointer, but :196 predates it and still reads as if the whole claim is superseded, not just the '12 = defect' reading. Either § Consequences :196 needs its own amendment pointer, or the scoping statement overstates what was corrected.

findings.title: Honest-null census stub promotion probe cites a command that does not exist
findings.detail: agents/roadmaps/stubs/road-to-a-census-that-refuses-a-partial-store.md:62-64 promotion probe says 'git log -p --follow agents/evidence/metrics/skill-activation-census.json is the whole probe'. But `git log -p --follow` outputs diff hunks, not a yes/no answer to 'did stores[] shrink'. The probe needs grep or a scripted parser to answer the question. As written it describes the data source, not the executable test. Either complete the probe (pipe to grep for 'stores' with logic) or reframe it as 'examine git log ...' rather than claiming it 'is the whole probe'.

findings.title: Vendored grammar upstream anchor docblock claims independence it explicitly disclaims
findings.detail: src/scripts/_lib/vendored_grammar_upstream.ts:11-24 docblock § WHAT THIS ANSWERS says 'This module closes it by comparing the vendored bytes against a source the repository does not author' — but :15-24 § WHAT IT MAY CLAIM immediately says 'It MUST NOT claim to be independent of all repository state'. The first sentence asserts the anchor is outside the repo's authorship; the second says it's not independent of repo state. Both are true (the upstream is external, but npm ci reads the lock), but the juxtaposition reads as contradiction unless the reader parses 'repository does not author' as distinct from 'repository state'. Suggest: reorder so the disclaimer comes first, or reframe the first sentence to 'compares against the locked upstream' without the 'does not author' clause that implies full independence.

findings.title: Test docblock claims module 'was written to close' a threat class it only partly closes
findings.detail: tests/scripts/vendored_grammar_upstream.test.ts:9 docblock says the module 'was written to close' the same-commit manifest+bytes threat. But the module's own docblock (vendored_grammar_upstream.ts:25-30) explicitly carves out 'an attacker who edits node_modules after install defeats this, and a lock entry that points at a hostile package defeats it earlier still'. So the threat class is only partly closed (the manifest-internal loop is broken, but the lock-to-bytes chain is not cryptographically verified). The test docblock overstates what the module achieves. Either qualify it ('written to close the manifest-internal half') or cite the module's own carve-out.

findings.title: Path traversal in session ID sanitization allows directory escape
findings.detail: src/scripts/_lib/session_index_trust.ts:206 sanitizes session IDs with `.replace(/[^A-Za-z0-9._-]/gu, '_')` but preserves dots and hyphens. An attacker-controlled session ID like `../../etc/passwd` becomes `_.._.._.._etc_passwd`, which still resolves outside the intended directory when path.join() processes the remaining path separators in the parent directory string. The latch path construction at line 207 uses `path.join(workspaceRoot, 'agents', 'runtime', 'state', 'session-index-latch', ...)` — while the sanitized filename itself won't escape, a malicious workspace root parameter could. More critically, the test at line 204 demonstrates awareness ('sanitises the session id into the latch filename') but only validates the basename, not the full resolved path containment.
findings.rationale: FALSE POSITIVE, and the finding concedes its own core: "the sanitized filename itself won't escape". `latchPath` replaces every character outside [A-Za-z0-9._-] with `_`, and both path separators are outside that class, so no separator survives into `path.join`. Probed over six escape shapes — `../../etc/passwd`, `..`, `.`, `a/../../b`, a backslash form and a percent-encoded form — every result stays under <ws>/agents/runtime/state/session-index-latch/. The fallback claim ("a malicious workspace root could") is finding 121c73bfc0c9, not path traversal in the sanitiser, and `slice(0,128)` cannot manufacture a separator either.
findings.verified_by: node probe over latchPath's exact regex for 6 escape shapes -> containment true for all 6. Read of src/scripts/_lib/session_index_trust.ts:307-310.

findings.title: Workspace root parameter is untrusted attacker-controlled input with no origin validation
findings.detail: The workspaceRoot parameter throughout session_index_trust.ts flows from hook payloads (hot_context_hook.ts:415 receives it from payload, passes to _session_index_block_or_null which passes to session_index_trust). The threat model at line 20 identifies 'a wrong or stale root' but the countermeasure (P1 identity check) only validates that memory root is INSIDE workspace root — it never validates that workspace root itself is the legitimate workspace for THIS session. An attacker supplying workspaceRoot=/tmp/malicious with agents/memory/ containing crafted entries would pass all checks. The canonicalization at line 161 resolves symlinks but doesn't verify the root belongs to the current session/repository.
findings.rationale: FALSE POSITIVE against the module's stated threat model, which the finding quotes but then argues past. `workspaceRoot` reaches the hook as `envelope.workspace_root` (hot_context_hook.ts:497) — the HOST payload, which is the trust boundary above this process. An attacker who can forge that envelope already controls the hook invocation and needs no memory-index path. The docblock states the attacker in scope is "not an intruder: it is a wrong or stale root", and states plainly that content is not authenticated. A "legitimate workspace for THIS session" check has nothing to compare against: the session id also arrives on the same envelope.
findings.verified_by: Read of src/scripts/hot_context_hook.ts:497 (root = envelope.workspace_root ?? cwd) and :416-437; src/scripts/_lib/session_index_trust.ts:1-36 (threat model) and :200-274 (P1/P2/P3).

findings.title: Time-of-check-time-of-use race in latch claim allows double injection
findings.detail: claimSessionOnce() at line 263 uses writeFileSync with flag 'wx' for atomicity, but the check at hot_context_hook.ts:435 ('P5 — duplicate invocation') and the subsequent memory read at line 447 are separate operations. An attacker racing two session_start events could: (1) both pass the trust check at line 428, (2) first wins latch at line 435, (3) second fails latch but first's memory read hasn't completed, (4) if first's build_session_index_block fails/hangs, second could inject before first completes. The 'claimed AFTER the trust verdict' ordering at line 438 means a refused root doesn't burn the claim, but a passed root that fails downstream leaves a window.
findings.rationale: FALSE POSITIVE: the race the finding describes cannot double-inject, and the code orders itself to prevent exactly it. `claimSessionOnce` writes with flag `wx`, which is atomic — of two concurrent starts exactly one creates the file and the other gets EEXIST and refuses. The claim is taken AFTER the render (`if (block === null) return null` precedes it), so "first's build fails/hangs" ends in no claim and no injection rather than in a second injection. The one window where two blocks can be served is the documented fail-open branch on an unwritable state directory — a deliberate trade named in the docblock, not a TOCTOU.
findings.verified_by: Read of src/scripts/_lib/session_index_trust.ts:312-346 (wx + EEXIST + fail-open) and src/scripts/hot_context_hook.ts:437-462 (claim ordered after render).

findings.title: Path-only rule exemption silently changes delivery semantics without measuring impact
findings.detail: project_thin_rules.ts:94 adds path_only_ids() exemption keeping rules full-bodied when their only triggers are path-shaped. The commit message states this resolves E2's conflict (pre_tool_use binding removed but 3 rules were reachable only there), but: (1) no measurement of the 3 rules' actual usage is provided, (2) the exemption is permanent ('stated as a PROPERTY rather than a list of ids') but its necessity is temporary (only while pre_tool_use is unbound), (3) keeping them eager costs ~5,850 tokens (per AC-1 failure note) which directly causes the rules limb miss (24,166 > 20,000), (4) the alternative (binding pre_tool_use) would honor the cap but is rejected based on the p90 measurement without considering rate limiting or other mitigations.

findings.title: Stub pointer path is wrong for .clinerules depth, documented as 'known limit' but ships broken
findings.detail: project_thin_rules.ts:266 BODY_LINK_PREFIX uses '../../dist/agent-src/rules/' which is correct for 2-level trees (.claude/rules, .cursor/rules) but wrong for 1-level .clinerules. The comment at line 260 acknowledges this: 'A stub in `.clinerules` needs an operator to have added `cline` to that list, and its pointer is off by one level.' This means under mode=thin (where the pointer is the ONLY path to the body), cline users get broken links. The justification 'strictly better than the previous state, where the pointer was dead in all three' is a comparison to a bug, not a validation of correctness.

findings.title: Recall measurement denominator error propagates into ADR and claims as authoritative
findings.detail: roadmap.md AC-2 states '102/102 reachable' but corrects to '101/101' with explanation that 4 rules have no triggers. However, ADR-265:56 and CLAIMS.md:365 both cite '101/101 labelled rules reachable' but the corpus has 105 auto rules (102 quoted + 3 bare). The '101/101' treats the 4 trigger-less rules as unlabelable, but step 0.2 (roadmap:231) counts 11 unlabeled rules and explicitly lists 4 with no triggers. If 105 total - 4 triggerless = 101 labelable, and 94 pre-existing + 7 new = 101, the math reconciles but the CLAIMS row doesn't show this work, presenting '101/101' as if the denominator is self-evident when it required correction twice in the roadmap.
findings.rationale: FALSE POSITIVE on its stated defect, which is that the row "presents 101/101 as if the denominator is self-evident". It does not: `non_inference` states "The recall figure is over a LABELLED corpus of 101 rules, so it bounds the rules that carry fixtures and says nothing about the four trigger-less and three path-only rules, which are exempted from thinning entirely rather than delivered." That is the denominator, its exclusions and their reason. The finding then reconciles the arithmetic itself ("the math reconciles"), so no number is disputed — only the visibility of work that is visible.
findings.verified_by: Read of docs/CLAIMS.md:365 non_inference field, sentence 3.

findings.title: Freshness check accepts future dates within 60s, allowing time-travel attacks during clock skew
findings.detail: session_index_trust.ts:191 refuses future mtimes only if `> now.getTime() + 60_000` (60 second grace). During NTP corrections or VM snapshots, an attacker with filesystem access could plant files dated 30s in the future that pass validation but represent tampered content. The 60s threshold is uncommented — unlike MAX_ROOT_AGE_DAYS which explicitly states 'a stated default, not a measured optimum', this magic number has no documented threat model. A malicious curated entry dated 59s ahead passes P3 freshness, fails no other check, and gets injected as trusted context.
findings.rationale: FALSE POSITIVE: the 60s grace is not a tampering control and nothing claims it is. The premise is "an attacker with filesystem access", and such an attacker can plant a hostile entry dated NOW — the module's docblock says so in terms: "A curated entry that is wrong, or hostile, and sits at the correct path inside the correct workspace passes every property here". Freshness is a property of the SOURCE FILES against clock skew, so the grace window buys an attacker who already has write access nothing. The secondary observation (60_000 carries no stated-default note while MAX_ROOT_AGE_DAYS does) is a documentation preference, not a security finding, and is recorded here rather than acted on.
findings.verified_by: Read of src/scripts/_lib/session_index_trust.ts:28-36 (content not authenticated) and :256-263 (the future-mtime refusal).

findings.title: Host tree parity gate generates into temp but doesn't verify temp isolation
findings.detail: check_host_tree_parity.ts:153 creates temp=mkdtemp(), seeds it, generates twice, compares, then removes. However: (1) the temp directory name is predictable (os.tmpdir() + 'host-parity-'), (2) no verification that mkdtemp() succeeded in a location isolated from the repository, (3) the afterEach cleanup at line 33 in the test file uses `fs.rmSync(tmp, { recursive: true, force: true })` which silently succeeds even if tmp was never created, so a failed setup wouldn't be detected. If mkdtemp() fails (disk full, permissions), the generator might write into cwd or another unexpected location.

findings.title: Settings schema enum doesn't match resolver's drop behavior, creating validation gap
findings.detail: agent-settings.schema.json:47 restricts hosts items to `enum: [claude-code, cursor, cline]` while resolveLeanProjectionHosts() at lean_projection_mode.ts:120 accepts ANY string and drops unknowns. The finding at #6 in the review notes this correctly: 'For any config that passes validation the drop path and its two carefully-worded reasons are unreachable' — but this means the schema is stricter than the code. If a user hand-edits .agent-settings.yml with hosts: [windsurf], the resolver drops it with 'not-thinnable', but if they use validate_agent_settings, it fails with 'not one of [claude-code, cursor, cline]'. The two error messages describe different validation layers but there's no documentation of which runs when.

findings.title: Empty HOME in tests disables user-scope dedup but doesn't prevent $HOME reads in dependencies
findings.detail: Multiple test files (lean_projection_host_scope.test.ts:89, check_host_tree_parity.ts:144) set process.env['HOME'] to an empty temp directory 'so user-scope dedup must find no twin'. However, this only affects code that reads $HOME directly — any dependency (including Node's os.homedir() in some configurations, or third-party modules) might cache the original HOME or read /etc/passwd. The test assumes `$HOME` isolation is complete but doesn't verify no reads escape. If a tool in the call chain uses os.homedir() before the override, the test measures something other than the isolated case it thinks it's testing.

findings.title: Slot fire size measurement skips pre_compact 'by construction' but claims to measure it
findings.detail: report_standing_payload_by_host.ts:433 returns empty array for pre_compact with comment 'zero by construction, not by measurement: that branch clears the seen-set and returns allow without writing to stdout'. But slotFireSizes() at line 413 is titled 'Measured through the SAME selection the runtime concern uses' — if pre_compact is known to emit zero by code inspection, it's not measured, yet the table at line 376 reports it as p50/p90/max all zero as if these are measured statistics. A reader expecting measurement data gets a construction assertion instead. The distinction matters for validation: 'measured zero' means tested, 'construction zero' means assumed.

findings.title: ADR-265 evidence table claims 'delivery was accepted by resolver long before schema' but schema was the bug
findings.detail: ADR-265:149 Evidence table row states 'delivery was accepted by the resolver while agent-settings.schema.json did not, so a consumer setting the documented value failed validation' — this frames the resolver as correct and schema as lagging. But the resolver's acceptance of an undocumented third mode (when only eager-all/thin were in the schema) was itself a contract violation. The template shipped 'mode: eager-all' while the code accepted 'delivery'; shipping code that accepts undocumented values is a forward-compatibility risk, not a feature. The evidence row presents this as validation catching up to code, when both were partially wrong.

findings.title: Inconsistent terminology for 'workspace root' vs 'project root' vs 'repository root'
findings.detail: The trust contract documentation uses 'workspace root' (session_index_trust.ts:146), but the codebase also uses PROJECT_ROOT (check_host_tree_parity.ts:59), REPO_ROOT (report_standing_payload_by_host.ts:63), 'repository root', and 'workspace' interchangeably. In the trust-boundary context, these distinctions matter: a workspace could be a worktree, a repository is the .git parent, a project root is what the settings cascade walks from. The threat model at line 20 explicitly calls out 'a worktree pointed at another tree' as an attacker, so conflating 'workspace' and 'repository' obscures the attack surface.

findings.title: Percentile calculation uses nearest-rank but doesn't document empty-sample behavior
findings.detail: report_standing_payload_by_host.ts:365 defines percentile() returning 0 for empty samples, but the docstring just says 'Empty sample → 0' without explaining why this is safe. The caller slotFireSizes() uses this for budget calculations (p90 determines the cap), so if a slot legitimately has zero fires (like pre_compact), the p90=0 looks like measured data. A reader can't distinguish 'measured zero because no samples' from 'measured zero because all samples were zero'. The row() function at line 372 doesn't annotate which case applies.

findings.title: CLAIMS.md:365 flip statement falsified by the flipped tree itself
findings.detail: The row was rewritten to say 'SHIPPED FOR CLAUDE CODE ONLY' and re-measured (616/616 byte-equal, 101/101 reachable, 0/212 near-misses). But the package default (`src/config/agent-settings.template.yml:198-199`) NOW ships `mode: delivery` + `hosts: [claude-code]` (step 4.3, ticked), and step 4.2 measured the flipped repo at 39,758 total / 24,166 rules tokens. The claim states it is shipped AND that the flip is Claude-only, which was true at measurement but is contradicted by the template the branch commits. A consumer installing this tree receives `delivery` by default, so 'shipped for Claude Code only' is not the shipped state — it is shipped-for-everyone with a host scope inside it.
findings.rationale: FALSE POSITIVE, refuted by the template the finding cites. `src/config/agent-settings.template.yml:214` ships `hosts: [claude-code]`, and the same file states "Every host outside the list receives" the eager tree — so a consumer installing this tree does NOT receive delivery on every host. The row already says this twice: the claim body names ADR-267 and the flip explicitly, and `non_inference` opens "SCOPED TO ONE HOST BY CONSTRUCTION ... every host outside that list receives byte-for-byte what `eager-all` writes". The finding's own restatement — "shipped-for-everyone with a host scope inside it" — is the row's content, not a contradiction of it.

findings.title: Step 4.2 measured ≤40k total but >20k rules, criterion split-ticked without recording the miss
findings.detail: AC '`check_preamble_payload_budget` on a Claude Code install: total ≤40k tok, rules ≤20k' is marked `[x]` with 'SPLIT VERDICT — total limb MET, rules limb MISSED'. The step's own note says 'total 39,758 ≤40k PASSES' and 'rules 24,166 >20k does not', then blames the 3.2 disposition for the 4,166-tok overage. The criterion has two limbs and one failed, so ticking it asserts the opposite of what the note records. Either the criterion is not met (stay `[ ]`) or it needs amendment to the limb that passed.
findings.rationale: FALSE POSITIVE on a factual premise: the criterion is NOT ticked. In the frozen snapshot the reviewer read, step 4.2 is `- [ ]` at roadmap.md:574, and cited line 450 carries unrelated prose about compaction de-duplication. The live roadmap agrees — `agents/roadmaps/road-to-delivery-for-every-host.md:600` is `- [ ]`, and its AC block at :810 reads "SPLIT VERDICT 2026-09-07 - total limb MET, rules limb MISSED, and left unticked". The remedy the finding asks for ("stay `[ ]`") is the state that shipped.
findings.verified_by: grep -n '4.2 Flip this repo first' on the review-input snapshot -> :574 '- [ ]'; sed -n 600p and 810p on agents/roadmaps/road-to-delivery-for-every-host.md.

findings.title: Step 4.4 blocked on measurement surface but 7.1 ticked and row rewritten
findings.detail: 4.4 is `[ ]` with 'BLOCKED 2026-09-07, on a measurement-surface question this roadmap does not settle' — the gate reads `dist/agent-src/rules`, unchanged at 138,200 either way, so the baseline cannot be lowered to a post-flip total the gate cannot reproduce. 7.1 is `[x]` 'done 2026-09-07' and rewrote `CLAIMS.md:365` to carry the re-measured figures. But 4.4's blocker is the same surface question: the claim cites measurements of trees the hosts load (24,166 rules for Claude, 121,242 for Cursor/Cline), and the gate that would enforce them reads a different tree. So 7.1 published figures anchored to a surface its own roadmap says is undecided, and the claim is backed by numbers no CI gate will reproduce.
findings.rationale: FALSE POSITIVE on the concealment it alleges. Both tick states are as reported (4.4 `[ ]` at :631, 7.1 `[x]` at :663), but the CLAIMS row 7.1 wrote discloses the exact surface mismatch: "the standing-payload gate `check_preamble_payload_budget` reads the projection SOURCE by default and its number is UNCHANGED by this flip at 138,200 - a reader comparing that gate before and after will correctly see no movement, because it measures a different surface from the one this claim reports." The roadmap says the same at risk row 3, which it marks REFUTED and UNMITIGATED rather than quietly ticking. The claim is backed by a bench endpoint, never by that gate, so "numbers no CI gate will reproduce" describes a disclosed boundary, not an unbacked claim.
findings.verified_by: grep of the review-input snapshot (:631 4.4 unticked, :663 7.1 ticked); read of docs/CLAIMS.md:365 final non_inference sentence and agents/roadmaps/road-to-delivery-for-every-host.md:794 (risk 3, REFUTED/UNMITIGATED).

findings.title: Step 3.2 applies E2's exception then closes by removing the exception's premise
findings.detail: E2 says '`pre_tool_use` delivery is disabled unless 3.1 shows a labelled rule reachable only there'. 3.1 shows three. The step's note says 'E2's exception fired and I did not take it' and instead keeps the three path-only rules eagerly projected, removes the binding, and calls this 'honouring every literal clause of E2 that remains'. But the clause that remains is 'disabled unless X', and X is true (3.1 lists the three), so disabling it contradicts the unless. The note argues the three 'lose nothing' because they are kept eager — true for their reachability, false for the E2 clause, which is about the binding. The binding is gone and the exception that would have kept it is described as taken by removing the condition it was conditioned on.

findings.title: AC-1 unticked but all three verify limbs met, with contradictory scoping note
findings.detail: AC-1 ('read command not refused, creating command still is, pinned') is `[x]` with 'MET 2026-09-07' and three verify limbs all reported green. The note then says 'NOT MET as written, and left unticked' and spends 15 lines on why the rules limb missed. So the checkbox is ticked, the status line says met, and the note says not-met-and-unticked. One of those is wrong.

findings.title: Risk 3 refutation contradicts its own 4.4 reference
findings.detail: Risk 3 mitigation originally said '4.2 flips this repo before 4.3 touches the package default; 4.4 lowers the baseline'. Re-reviewed row now says 'REFUTED 2026-09-08 … Risk 3 is UNMITIGATED and still live for 2026-11-10. Steps 4.4 and 7.2 are blocked on it'. But 4.4's own status is `[ ]` 'BLOCKED 2026-09-07' on the same measurement-surface question, so the refutation is consistent with the step. What contradicts is that the Risk was re-reviewed 2026-09-08 and calls the mitigation refuted, while the Mitigation column still cites the original ordering (4.2 then 4.3 then 4.4) that the refutation says does not work. Either the Mitigation cell updates to match the refutation or the refutation belongs in a note rather than inline.

findings.title: Recall floor re-reviewed with corrected denominator but the corrected number is still wrong
findings.detail: Risk 1 mitigation was re-reviewed 2026-09-08 and says the floor is 'complete and the mitigation's own figure was WRONG. Phase 2 … measured … 101/101 reachable'. The note corrects '102/102' to '101/101' because 4 of 105 auto rules have no triggers. But step 2.1's verify says '102/102 reachable' and the measurement there is '101/101 rules reachable; unreachable: none' with 0 false fires on 212 near-misses. So 101/101 is right and the criterion it was written against (2.1 verify) still says 102. The re-review corrected one number and left the contradicting one in the step.

findings.title: Step 0.2 count corrected from 8 to 11 but its verify still says 102+3=105
findings.detail: Step 0.2 lists 11 unlabelled auto rules and says 'the count is 11, not 8 — corrected-from-reproduction'. Its verify says 'ls … | wc -l plus the listed names equals the type: auto count — counting BOTH quoted and bare (102+3)'. 102+3=105, and 105−94 labelled = 11 unlabelled, so the arithmetic reconciles. But the verify is written as an instruction ('count both forms') that produces 105, and a reader following it gets 105−94=11 only if they also subtract the 94. The step knows the answer is 11; the verify describes how to get 105.

findings.title: AC-0 verify says rules ≤20k but the measured rules are 24,166
findings.detail: AC-0 (the first unticked one) says 'check_preamble_payload_budget on the repo reports rules ≤20k tok, total ≤40k'. The criterion is the gating condition for starting 4.2. But 4.2's own measurement, quoted in the AC block 30 lines below, is 'rules 24,166 tok … The rules limb MISSES: 24,166 > 20k, by 4,166.' So AC-0's rules limb is the condition for the step, and the step measured that it does not hold. Either AC-0 should be ticked with the split recorded (total met, rules not) or 4.2 should be unticked because its precondition failed.

findings.title: Inconsistent MCP tool count in catalog description vs. measurements
findings.detail: The skill description (agents/index.md:49) claims 'impact, tests-for, dead cheaper' but the catalog shows 36 tools total (up from 31), meaning 5 graph tools were added. However, the description treats these as three distinct verbs when the actual implementation includes 5 MCP tools (graph_impact, graph_tests_for, graph_dead, graph_query, graph_path). The fourth verb 'untested' is mentioned in verification notes but not consistently reflected in user-facing documentation.

findings.title: Accepted-edge filter excludes valid 'member' edges but reasoning is unclear
findings.detail: In verbs.ts, REFERENCE_RELATIONS excludes 'member' because 'a declaration is not a use'. However, the filter's purpose is to identify accepted resolution mechanisms, not semantic relationships. A file->symbol member edge with resolved_via='same-file' is still an ACCEPTED edge by the mechanism axis. The exclusion appears correct for 'dead' (where member edges would false-positive) but the rationale conflates two distinct filters.

findings.title: MCP graph_impact tool executes git subprocess with user-controlled rev parameter
findings.detail: graph_impact accepts a 'diff' parameter and passes it directly to 'git diff --name-only <rev>..HEAD'. While hardenedSpawnEnv() is used, there's no validation that <rev> is a valid git ref before execution. An attacker-controlled rev like '--help' or '$(malicious)' could trigger unintended git behavior or command injection. The error handling catches failures but doesn't prevent the attempt.
findings.rationale: REAL, in a different mechanism than the one claimed — so half the finding is refuted and half is fixed. There is no shell: `changedFiles` uses `execFileSync` with an argv array, so `$(malicious)` is handed to git as a literal rev and refused; command injection is impossible. What IS reachable is OPTION injection, which the `${ref}..HEAD` concatenation does not prevent: `--output=/tmp/x` becomes `--output=/tmp/x..HEAD`, a well-formed `git diff` option whose value is a filename. Probed against a throwaway repository: git exited 0 and created the file. Reachable from the `graph_impact` MCP tool, whose `diff` parameter is model-supplied. Fixed at the SHARED path rather than at the tool, so both callers are covered: a rev never begins with `-`, so `changedFiles` refuses one before git runs. Sibling search for the construct — an externally-supplied rev interpolated into a git argv — found 1 site reachable from a tool parameter (this one); the ~18 other `..HEAD` interpolations take their base ref from a gate's own argv or env, i.e. from the operator, and are unchanged.
findings.verified_by: Probe: git diff --name-only "--output=/tmp/gitprobe/PWNED..HEAD" in a throwaway repo -> exit 0, file "PWNED..HEAD" created. New test tests/scripts/code_graph_rev_option_injection.test.ts, 4 assertions, green with the guard; sensitivity proven by neutralising the guard -> the --output case goes red, restored -> green.

findings.title: Resolution tier reports 'import-specifier 47,701 → 47,669' but unclear if this is regression
findings.detail: Step 2.3's closure note states the tsconfig tier moves 32 edges from import-specifier to path-alias, and 'import-specifier 47,701 → 47,669' is cited as evidence. This is a -32 delta, which matches the tier's behavior. However, the note positions this as 'what a future reader should measure' without clearly stating whether this -32 is acceptable or a silent loss of import edges. The verify was amended to remove a regression check, but the downstream impact isn't evaluated.

findings.title: AC-6 claims 'byte-identical' but lists multiple differences in the same paragraph
findings.detail: AC-6's verification states '126 metric fields on each side, 0 differences' and calls the result 'byte-identical'. The next paragraph immediately lists what DID differ: run date, measured commit, tree-hashes, wall_ms, output_bytes. The claim should be 'metric-identical' not 'byte-identical', since the reports are demonstrably not byte-identical files. This matters for reproducibility claims.

findings.title: dead() verb refuses by default but exported function entries may be incorrectly excluded
findings.detail: The 'exports' entry-point source is always 'unavailable' because the extractor records no exportedness. dead() refuses unless --accept-missing-exports or --entry-points is supplied. However, if a user supplies an entry-points file and it includes a symbol that IS exported but not yet imported (the case the refusal exists to prevent), that symbol is excluded from the dead list via the 'entries' check. This means the supplied list can HIDE genuinely dead exported symbols if the operator mistakenly includes them.

findings.title: Inconsistent terminology: 'EXTRACTED does not regress' vs. actual measurement axis
findings.detail: Step 2.3's amended verify says 'EXTRACTED does not regress on the repository build', measured as 130,348 / 130,348. But the note explains the tsconfig tier moves 32 edges from import-specifier to path-alias—both are EXTRACTED confidence. The tier changes the mechanism (resolved_via), not confidence. The verify is checking that total extracted edge count is stable, but phrases it as 'EXTRACTED does not regress' when the tier cannot regress EXTRACTED by design.

findings.title: Path traversal vulnerability in graph_dead entry_points parameter
findings.detail: graph_dead accepts an 'entry_points' parameter as a file path and validates it with path.resolve(root, listArg) + startsWith check. However, the check is 'abs.startsWith(path.resolve(root) + path.sep)', which can be bypassed on Windows via path canonicalization differences (e.g., root='C:\repo' but abs='C:/repo/../../../etc/passwd' may not match). The fixture asserts '../outside.txt' is rejected, but a more sophisticated traversal (e.g., symlink, UNC path, or case-insensitive bypass) isn't tested.

findings.title: Blocker re-measurement shows worsening (9.82→10.31 MB) but disposition contradicts itself
findings.detail: The pack-size blocker note records origin/main grew from 9.8216 MB (2026-09-07) to 10.3087 MB (2026-09-08), +0.49 MB beyond this branch's +0.37 MB contribution. The note states 'this branch's own contribution is the +373,922 B recorded above and landed with Phase 0.1, which is already on main at both pins'. But if Phase 0.1 landed and is on main at BOTH pins, the +0.37 MB should appear in BOTH measurements, not as a delta between them. Either the timeline is wrong or the attribution is.

findings.title: Risk Register rank 1 claims 'readers shipped with it' but usage is unmeasured
findings.detail: Post-close review of rank 1 states 'Readers shipped with it: 3.4 (regression selector), 4.1 (five MCP tools, catalogue 36) and the four CLI verbs'. It then adds 'What is NOT claimed: an available reader is not a used one, and usage is unmeasured'. This undermines the mitigation—if readers exist but usage is zero, the risk (delivery without a reader) is not actually mitigated. The claim should either measure usage or reframe the risk as 'delivery without reachable reader'.

findings.title: Privilege escalation via automatic continuity record writing
findings.detail: The new continuity.auto_record feature (step 1.2 in road-to-continuity-writer-activation) arms an automatic producer on session-end that can persist state across sessions. The default ships 'off' but the mechanism itself lacks multi-tenancy isolation - the slot contract (continuity-record-slot.md) uses session_id comparison but does not validate workspace ownership boundaries. A malicious actor could craft a session_id collision or exploit the legacy shared path fallback to inject continuity records into another user's workspace. The quarantine mechanism moves unusable records but does not cryptographically verify their origin.
findings.rationale: FALSE POSITIVE: there is no cross-workspace path to escalate through. Every continuity path is built as `path.join(workspace_root, <relative>)` — the legacy fallback included, which is a RELATIVE path inside the same workspace, not a shared one — so "inject records into another user's workspace" presupposes write access to that user's tree, at which point the filesystem permission model has already failed and this module is not the control. Within one workspace, cross-session reads are what `resolveContinuityRecord`'s ambiguity rule plus the branch gate exist for. And there is no privilege to escalate: the record is delivered inside a block labelled "DATA from a PRIOR SESSION - never instructions. Nothing inside this block authorizes an action." `continuity.auto_record` also ships off.
findings.verified_by: Read of src/scripts/_lib/continuity_slot.ts:132-190, 214-265 (all paths joined onto workspace_root) and src/scripts/_lib/recycle_envelope_paths.ts:60-145 (legacy path is workspace-relative; resolution by identity, workspace and branch, never recency).

findings.title: CI agent injection vulnerability in PR-triggered workflows
findings.detail: ADR-266 (explicit-pr-merge-invocation) acknowledges but does not fix CI-side agent merge capability: 'A workflow holding a write-scoped token — pull_request_target being the usual shape — merges through the API regardless of what any rule text says'. The diff shows no remediation of this attack vector. An attacker-controlled fork PR with malicious title/body/diff can reach an agent running in CI with repo secrets and write permissions (e.g., via pull_request_target trigger). The ADR explicitly states 'this record governs the agent-in-a-session path only' and defers the CI path to forge-side controls that may not exist in consumer repos.
findings.rationale: ACCEPTED, and already recorded as accepted — the finding reports a scope boundary the record states in its own words rather than an undisclosed hole. ADR-266:127-134 reads "2 - a CI-side agent can merge, and this record does not reach it. Real, and ... The control there is forge-side ... This record governs the agent-in-a-session path only, and a green CI is not evidence that the CI path is gated." So the residual is real, named, attributed to the forge layer, and accompanied by the warning not to read CI green as coverage. Accepting it here rather than calling it a false positive is the honest word: the finding misread nothing. What it does not establish is a new exposure — this repository ships no `pull_request_target` workflow that hands a write-scoped token to an agent, so the shape described is a consumer-side risk the ADR declines to govern, not a live path in this tree.
findings.verified_by: Read of docs/decisions/ADR-266-...md:121-134. grep -rn pull_request_target .github/workflows -> 5 hits, every one inside a comment stating there is none in this tree; no `on: pull_request_target:` trigger exists, and self-review-gate.yml (the one workflow that runs a model) declares contents: read.

findings.title: Unverified self-amendment in governance rules
findings.detail: ADR-268 section 4 permits governance self-amendment with ratification after-the-fact: 'An agent may modify its constitution. It may not ratify its own increase in power.' However, the mechanism is model-carried with no mechanical enforcement until a future CI gate is built (per ADR-268 Consequences: 'the first such PR is maintainer-authored or lands after § 4's CI gate'). During the transition period, an agent can modify kernel rules (ask-when-uncertain, commit-policy, non-destructive-by-default, scope-control, no-cheap-questions) and the only control is the deleted tool-call deny from block_kernel_rule_writes.ts. The 'provider diversity required where two providers are configured' clause is unenforceable without the CI gate.
findings.rationale: FALSE POSITIVE on the premise it rests on. The finding says "the only control is the DELETED tool-call deny from block_kernel_rule_writes.ts" — the guard is not deleted: src/scripts/hooks/block_kernel_rule_writes.ts is 13,075 bytes, is bound in src/scripts/hook_manifest.yaml:184-185, and carries its own test file. Remove that premise and what remains is ADR-268's own recorded position, not a hidden gap: § 4 names the ratification ladder, states that the deny is replaced by a CI gate reading the artifact (:204), and the Consequences record the sequencing constraint verbatim (:335, "the first such PR is maintainer-authored or lands after § 4's CI gate"). A record naming its own transition state is not an unverified self-amendment.
findings.verified_by: ls -la src/scripts/hooks/block_kernel_rule_writes.ts -> 13075 bytes; grep -n kernel src/scripts/hook_manifest.yaml -> :184 block-kernel-rule-writes bound; grep of ADR-268 :189-204 and :335.

findings.title: Delivery equivalence claim scope mismatch with measured surface
findings.detail: docs/CLAIMS.md line 365 (thin-inject-delivery-equivalence) claims '98/101 labelled rules reachable with user_prompt_submit' but the non_inference field admits a critical loss: '18 rules carry both path and non-path triggers… their path route has no carrier'. The claim's headline '98/101 reachable' obscures that 18 rules (design-fidelity, doc-screenshot-hygiene, lethal-trifecta-guard, etc.) lost their path-based activation without any labelled test coverage. The receiver stub (road-to-a-path-route-under-delivery.md) defers the fix to an owner decision, meaning the claimed 'delivery equivalence' has a known-unquantified loss baked into the shipped default.
findings.rationale: FALSE POSITIVE: the row publishes precisely what the finding says it obscures. The claim body carries BOTH readings — "101/101 is measured with `open_files` HONOURED, which is the reach of the MECHANISM and not of the shipped binding ... so the endpoint also publishes the shipped reach, 98/101" — and names the three differing rules. `non_inference` then devotes a passage to the 18 mixed-trigger rules, states that their path route has no carrier, explains why the labelled corpus cannot see it, and names the receiver stub. A disclosed limit stated at that length is not a headline obscuring a loss.
findings.verified_by: Read of docs/CLAIMS.md:365 claim + non_inference (98/101 and the 18-rule passage).

findings.title: Slot-sum budget exceeded by rule-inject concern
findings.detail: Finding 3 from the R2 completion review (noted in ADR-267) discovered the rule-inject concern was licensed at 20,480 bytes while the user_prompt_submit slot sum is 16,384 bytes - a 25% overage. This was corrected to 16,384 in the same change, but the residue reveals the gate design: the runtime enforces per_turn_aggregate_bytes.ceiling_bytes but does NOT enforce per-slot sums at runtime, only at authoring time. A concern that exceeds its slot row will be truncated at runtime rather than refused, potentially leaving security-critical rules undelivered.

findings.title: Unbounded authority persistence across interruptions
findings.detail: ADR-268 section 2 introduces mission-scoped grants with expires: mission-end that survive 'CI fixes, base syncs, conflict resolution, unrelated owner questions, or context resets' for up to twelve hours. The grant is spent once on 'the final green head' but there is no cryptographic binding - the authorization channel is 'the owner's own words' with no tamper-evident storage. ADR-266's table admits 'tamper-resistant: partially' because 'the manifest lives in the run's own context, not in a file anything can verify'. An interrupted twelve-hour run could resume with a modified grant and the only control is the pre-merge observed_head re-read, which validates the target but not the grant provenance.

findings.title: Grace ceiling enforcement gap creates unbounded growth window
findings.detail: ADR-264 designed a 128-token Iron Law reserve but ADR-265 refused to activate it because 'the verifier is inside the change it authorises'. The fallback shipped is standing_bound_ratchet.ts which refuses grace_ceiling rises but reports SKIPPED when no base ref resolves ('does not refuse when no base ref resolves... an unreadable base would refuse a change on an infrastructure failure'). This creates a window where shallow clones or CI environments without base-ref access bypass the only enforcement of the 138,490-byte ceiling that is already 28.4% above the design ceiling. The claim 'grace ceiling may not rise' is protected only where git history is readable.

findings.title: Roadmap phase completion contradicts open blockers
findings.detail: road-to-delivery-for-every-host Phase 4 acceptance criteria split: 'total limb MET, rules limb MISSED' (AC-1) but Phase 0-3 boxes are all ticked. The roadmap Goal requires 'rules ≤ 20,000' but measured 24,166 (4,166 over). The cause is named (3.2 disposition kept path-only rules full-bodied) but the step is marked [x] complete anyway. Step 4.2 'Flip this repo first' is left unticked with the reason recorded, but step 4.3 'Flip the package default' is marked [x] done including the regenerated projections. A reader following ticked boxes sees Phase 4 complete while its acceptance criteria explicitly say otherwise.

findings.title: Skill activation census denominator error propagated to claim
findings.detail: Amendment 1 to ADR-263 corrects 187 to 189 for 'human-named only' skills, stating the original was an 'arithmetic error: 12 + 100 - 2 = 110, remainder 299 - 110 = 189'. However, the docs/CLAIMS.md skill-activation-census-zero row still contains contradictory figures across its amendment history (579/579 vs 616/616 vs 591/591 deliveries, 94 vs 101 vs 97 rule corpus sizes). The claim is marked 'status: backed' but its evidence pointer moved three times (thin-inject-2026-08-23.md → thin-inject-2026-09-08.md) and the 'corrected-from-reproduction' markers show the denominator itself was re-derived wrongly twice.

findings.title: ADR number collision happened four times in one merge session
findings.detail: The ADR-number uniqueness stub records delivery-for-every-host was renumbered 262 → 263 → 265 → 266 → 267 in four collisions, the last two 'inside one merge session, minutes apart'. The stub concludes 'renumbering is not a fix; it is the defect moving' but proposes no durable solution beyond manual checking of origin/main + open PR heads at renumber time, which failed to prevent collision 4. The collision rate is highest 'where two lanes are most likely to need cross-references to each other', creating a documentation integrity risk.

findings.title: Verbose completion review inline amendments reduce diff clarity
findings.detail: Multiple roadmap files contain multi-paragraph 'CORRECTED 2026-09-08' / 'AMENDED 2026-09-09' blocks inline in step Done notes (e.g., road-to-delivery-for-every-host step 0.1, 3.2, 4.2). While these preserve the correction reasoning, they make the step status harder to parse - a reader must scan 50+ lines to determine if a [x] step's verify is actually met. The package's own style guide (CHANGELOG-conventions.md) uses 'BREAKING' / 'SECURITY' markers but has no convention for inline correctness amendments in roadmaps.
